definition.text: Latency is the time delay between a cause and its effect in a system, such as the wait between sending a request and seeing the response.

facts.text: Latency is physically a consequence of the limited speed at which any interaction can propagate, which never exceeds the speed of light, so any system with distance between cause and effect has some latency.
The precise definition of latency depends on the system being observed.
In communications, the lower limit of latency is set by the medium used to transfer the information.
Perceptible latency strongly affects user satisfaction and usability, and for high-scale user-facing systems high latency means a big loss of revenue.
Networks with relatively small delays are called low-latency networks, and the others are high-latency networks.
Mechanical latency is limited by physics: a disk read waits for the arm's seek time and then for the platter's rotational latency.
In multitasking computers, execution of a process can be postponed while other processes run, and the operating system schedules when each action happens, which adds software latency.

definition.text: Network latency is the delay for data to cross a network, measured one-way from source to destination or as the round-trip delay time.

facts.text: Network latency is measured either one-way, from the source sending a packet to the destination receiving it, or as round-trip delay time; round-trip is quoted more often because it can be measured from a single point.

Ping measures round-trip delay roughly with an ICMP echo request, but not accurately, since ICMP is for diagnostics and routers may shape different protocols differently; tools such as hping, Netperf and Iperf measure better.
A packet crosses several links and gateways that each wait for the whole packet, so minimal latency is the sum of each link's transmission delay plus each gateway's forwarding latency.

In practice latency also includes queuing delay, when a gateway receives several packets for the same destination and some must wait, and processing delay while the gateway decides what to do with a packet.
Propagation, serialization, queuing and processing delays combine into a complex, variable latency profile, and bufferbloat can raise latency by an order of magnitude or more.
Light in optical fiber travels at about two thirds of its vacuum speed, which works out to about 5.0 μs of latency per kilometer; in a vacuum light takes 3.33 μs per kilometer.
Fiber rarely runs in a straight line, and amplifiers or regenerators added beyond 100 kilometers add their own latency.
A geostationary satellite adds about a quarter of a second each way, while a low Earth orbit satellite 400 km up adds about 12 ms.

definition.text: Tail latency is the high-percentile response time of a system, usually measured at the 95th, 99th or 99.9th percentile rather than as an average.

facts.text: Average and median latency can mislead in software systems, because a few outliers distort them.
Tail latency is the high-percentile response time, usually measured at the 95th, 99th or 99.9th percentile, not the average.
In distributed systems, cloud computing and large-scale web services, even a small number of slow requests can make user experience and system performance much worse.
Tail latency often comes from resource contention, network variability, garbage collection pauses and hardware heterogeneity.
Managing tail latency is a major design problem because lowering average latency does not always improve worst-case performance.
Common ways to lessen tail latency are request hedging, replication, load balancing and adaptive timeouts.
It matters most for search engines, financial systems and real-time services, where service-level objectives are often based on high-percentile latencies.
Monitoring built on the mean misleads: a web service with a 100 ms average latency at 1,000 requests per second may have 1% of requests taking 5 seconds.

definition.text: Network throughput is the rate at which messages are successfully delivered over a communication channel.

facts.text: Throughput is usually measured in bits per second, and sometimes in packets per second; aggregate throughput is the sum of the data rates delivered over all channels in a network.
Bandwidth is the maximum achievable speed or capacity, while throughput is the speed actually achieved and is always less than bandwidth.

Throughput is limited by the physical medium, the processing power of system components and end-user behavior; protocol overhead can make the useful rate much lower than the maximum achievable throughput.
If a link with data rate R is shared by N active users, each can ideally achieve about R/N, and router and switch schedulers decide how the bandwidth is actually shared.
Without fair queuing, users that send large packets get more bandwidth, while weighted fair queuing can prioritize some users when differentiated quality of service is provided.
Channel efficiency is the percentage of a channel's net bit rate that goes to achieved throughput: 70 Mbit/s over a 100 Mbit/s Ethernet connection is 70%.

definition.text: Four values describe the upper limit of what a system can deliver: maximum theoretical, asymptotic, peak measured and maximum sustained throughput.

facts.text: Maximum throughput is the highest data rate a system can deliver and is used most often to compare systems; the four upper-limit values mean different things, so comparisons must use the same definitions.

Maximum theoretical throughput is the most data that could be sent under ideal circumstances, closely related to channel capacity, and is reported more accurately once format and specification overhead are included.

Peak measured throughput is measured on a real or simulated system over a short period, also called instantaneous throughput; it suits burst transmission but is less useful for high duty-cycle systems.
Maximum sustained throughput is averaged over a long time and is likely the most accurate indicator of performance for networks under constant load.

definition.text: Goodput is the amount of useful information delivered per second to the application layer protocol.

facts.text: Maximum throughput is often an unreliable measure of effective bandwidth, because achieved throughput is usually lower and protocol overhead eats into it.
Goodput excludes dropped packets, retransmissions and protocol overhead, so it is lower than the maximum throughput.
In file transmission, goodput is the file size in bits divided by the file transmission time.

title: Latency vs throughput

definition.text: Latency is how long one operation takes, while throughput is how many operations complete per unit of time, and one does not determine the other.

facts.text: A passenger's trip time on the London to New York air link is the same whether 100 or 10000 passengers a day make the trip, so latency is independent of throughput.
Throughput is counted in messages per second, the reciprocal of the unit for propagation delay, seconds per message.
In reliable two-way communication, latency limits total throughput, as described by the bandwidth-delay product.
TCP flow control lowers throughput when the bandwidth-delay product is larger than the TCP window, because the sender must wait for acknowledgements before sending more packets.
A cache can benefit latency, throughput or both.
Beyond partitions, distributed systems face a trade-off between latency and consistency, as the PACELC theorem states.

notes: No page of its own; the comparison is assembled from the Latency and Network throughput pages and the Cache and CAP theorem pages (curriculum test: mentioned on several in-scope pages).

title: Design trade-offs

definition.text: Design trade-offs mean there is no right or wrong system design: every design is a compromise between competing goals.

facts.text: There is no right or wrong design: everything in system design is a trade-off and a compromise.
Important trade-offs include cost versus performance, reliability versus scalability, performance versus consistency, security versus flexibility, and development speed versus quality.
Scaling vertically means adding resources such as CPU and RAM to an existing server, while scaling horizontally means adding more servers to the pool.

SQL databases organize data into tables of rows and columns, while NoSQL suits applications that need a flexible schema. Normalization stores each piece of information once; denormalization combines data into fewer tables for faster queries.

Consistency promises the most recent data every time, while availability keeps the system up even when parts fail. Strong consistency reflects updates immediately; eventual consistency delays them across nodes.
Batch processing collects data and handles it at once, such as daily billing, while stream processing handles data in real time, such as fraud detection.
Synchronous processing performs tasks one after another, while asynchronous tasks can run in the background and new tasks start without waiting.

REST gathers data from multiple endpoints, while GraphQL fetches data more efficiently with specific queries at a higher design cost. A stateful system remembers past interactions; a stateless one does not.

notes: Hub entry over three ByteByteGo trade-off guides; each pair has a chapter or entry of its own elsewhere. Read-through vs write-through cache (966299c7726e, cd3e9159b0a6) left to the caching chapter.

title: Reducing latency

definition.text: Latency is lowered with a handful of standard techniques: database indexing, load balancing, a content delivery network, async processing and data compression.

facts.text: For high-scale user-facing systems high latency is a big loss of revenue; the top strategies to reduce it are database indexing, load balancing, a content delivery network, async processing and data compression.

Round-trip time is twice the network latency plus processing at the destination; propagation time depends on distance and more bandwidth does not reduce it, so the remaining delay is increasingly propagation.
A CDN is a geographically distributed network of proxy servers and data centers; its edge servers sit closer to the end user than traditional servers, which reduces latency.
A cache benefits latency, throughput or both, and prefetching that guesses future reads and requests them ahead of time bypasses the latency altogether if done optimally.
A database index speeds up data retrieval on a table, at the cost of additional writes and storage space to maintain the index.
Load balancing distributes tasks over resources to make overall processing more efficient, optimizing response time and avoiding overloading some nodes while others sit idle.
Async processing through a message queue lets producers add requests without waiting for them to be processed, so new tasks can start without waiting for earlier ones.
Content codings let a representation be compressed without losing information, and HTTP compression with gzip reduces the amount of data transferred for HTTP objects.

notes: Replaces the thin first-round entry. The ByteByteGo guide only names the five strategies, so each one is explained from the CDN, cache, database index, load balancing, message queue and RFC 9110 pages. Hedged requests and multiplexed requests are kept as mentions.

title: Back-of-the-envelope estimation

definition.text: Back-of-the-envelope estimation is a rough calculation built on simplified assumptions that sizes a system's users, traffic and storage before it is designed.

facts.text: A back-of-the-envelope calculation is more than a guess but less than an accurate calculation or proof, and its defining characteristic is the use of simplified assumptions.

Physicist Enrico Fermi emphasized approximating complex problems within an order of magnitude using simple calculations; such sample calculations are called Fermi questions or back-of-the-envelope calculations.
Estimating the scale of the system means asking about desired scale, the read/write ratio, requests per second and storage needed; these answers help scale the design later.
Capacity estimation focuses on the number of users, traffic, storage and memory needs, and compute and networking requirements.
The primer advises clarifying with the interviewer whether to run back-of-the-envelope usage calculations at all.
A handy conversion guide says a month has about 2.5 million seconds, so 1 request per second is 2.5 million requests per month.
In the same guide, 40 requests per second equal 100 million requests per month, and 400 requests per second equal 1 billion requests per month.
Storage per record comes from adding up its fields: 1 KB of content, a 7-byte shortlink, a 4-byte expiration length, a 5-byte creation time and a 255-byte path make about 1.27 KB per paste.

notes: Replaces the first-round entry: adds the Wikipedia definition and the order-of-magnitude idea. The Pastebin example's 12.7 GB per month, 450 GB in 3 years, 4 writes and 40 reads per second were dropped to the mentions (they belong to the Pastebin worked example). The conversion guide repeats in all eight primer solutions; cited from the Pastebin one. Fermi's bomb test, radar and other anecdotes and the napkin-design trivia were skipped.

title: Latency numbers to know

definition.text: Rough latencies of common operations, from cache reads taking nanoseconds to a transatlantic packet taking 100 ms, let a designer judge which steps of a system are slow.

facts.text: These latency numbers are not accurate; they come from online benchmarks, including Jeff Dean's latency numbers, plus other sources.
L1 and L2 caches take 1 ns and 10 ns and are usually built onto the microprocessor chip; unless you work with hardware directly, you probably do not need to worry about them.
RAM access takes about 100 ns, and since Redis is an in-memory data store the guide puts a Redis read at about 100 ns as well.
Sending 1K bytes over a 1 Gbps network takes about 10 us, for example sending 1 KB of data from Memcached through the network.
Reading from an SSD takes about 100 us, for example a read from RocksDB, a disk-based key-value store.
A database insert takes about 1 ms, since the database must store the data, create the index and flush logs; a Postgresql commit might take 1 ms.
Sending a packet from California to the Netherlands and back takes about 100 ms, like the delay on a long-distance Zoom call.
Retry or refresh intervals are on the order of 1-10 s; a monitoring system's refresh interval is usually 5~10 seconds, the Grafana default.

notes: The guide itself says the numbers are not accurate. S:a5f33adf836e equates a Redis read with a RAM read (about 100 ns) and ignores the network trip to a Redis server; kept as the guide states it, flagged for verification. The primer solutions only point to 'Latency numbers every programmer should know' (S:ab6d1bca13ab) without listing numbers.

definition.text: Website performance is judged by nine metrics: load time, time to first byte, request count, DOMContentLoaded, above-the-fold load time, first contentful paint, page size, round trip time and render-blocking resources.

facts.text: Load time is how long the browser takes to download and display the webpage, measured in milliseconds.
Time to first byte (TTFB) is how long the browser waits to receive the first byte from the web server, and it shows the server's general ability to handle traffic.
Request count is the number of HTTP requests the browser must make to load the page fully; the lower it is, the faster the site feels.
DOMContentLoaded is the time for the full HTML to load, not counting CSS and other assets; the sooner it happens, the sooner users see useful functionality.

Above-the-fold content, the part of the page that fits in the browser window without scrolling, is seen first and often decides whether users keep reading; first contentful paint is when any content, text, image or background color, is first painted.
Page size is the total file size of all content and assets on the page; the bigger the page, the longer it takes to load.
Round trip time is a request going from the browser to the origin server plus the response coming back, and reducing it is a key way to improve a website's performance.
Render-blocking resources stop other parts of the page from loading, so the more a page has, the greater the delay, and their number should be tracked.

title: Bandwidth

definition.text: In computing, bandwidth is the maximum rate of data transfer across a given path.

facts.text: Bandwidth may be called network, data or digital bandwidth, which differs from signal bandwidth, the frequency range in hertz used in signal processing and wireless communications.
The term sometimes means net bit rate, peak bit rate, channel capacity or the maximum throughput of a communication path; bandwidth tests measure the maximum throughput of a network.
Consumed bandwidth in bit/s corresponds to achieved throughput or goodput, the average rate of successful data transfer.

A channel of x bit/s may not carry data at rate x, since protocols, encryption and other factors add overhead; TCP's three-way handshake for each transaction adds overhead, and lost packets cut useful throughput further.
Useful throughput is less than or equal to the actual channel capacity minus implementation overhead.
Because bandwidth spikes can skew a measurement, carriers often use the 95th percentile method, which continuously measures usage and removes the top 5 percent.
In web hosting, bandwidth often means the data transferred to or from a site in a period, such as gigabytes per month; the more accurate phrase is monthly data transfer.
Maximum physical-layer speeds of common links are 100 Mbit/s for Fast Ethernet, 1 Gbit/s for Gigabit Ethernet, 10 Gbit/s for 10 Gigabit Ethernet and 100 Gbit/s for 100 Gigabit Ethernet.

notes: Usage differs by source: Network throughput calls bandwidth the maximum capacity and throughput the achieved rate; this page also uses 'consumed bandwidth' for achieved throughput. Both stated, not a conflict. Edholm's law (bandwidth doubling every 18 months, S:108df395327e) and the MOSFET history were left out.

definition.text: Data sizes are expressed as multiples of the bit and the byte, using either decimal or binary prefixes.

facts.text: A byte means 8 bits today, though it once varied with hardware design; a more accurate but less common name for 8 bits is octet.

Decimal prefixes such as kilo- are commonly used with bit and byte, but hardware sizes are usually binary, so each prefix 1000^n is customarily used for a close approximation of 1024^n, which can cause confusion.
The IEC binary prefixes, such as kibi-, describe hardware sizes accurately but are not commonly used.
In decimal units a kilobyte is 1,000 bytes and each step up multiplies by 1,000 up to the petabyte, 1,000 terabytes; a kibibyte is 1,024 bytes and a mebibyte is 1,024 kibibytes.

title: Percentile

definition.text: A percentile is a value that is greater than a given percentage of all the values in a sample, so the 97th percentile is above 97% of the data points.

facts.text: The k-th percentile is above about k% of the sample; the 50th percentile is the median, and the 25th and 75th are the quartiles. A percentile is stated in the unit of the measured values, not in percent.

There is no standard definition of percentile: methods either return a score that exists in the data (nearest rank) or interpolate between scores, and all give similar results when the sample is very large.
With the nearest-rank method a percentile is always a member of the original list, and on lists with fewer than 100 distinct values one value can stand for more than one percentile.
Internet providers bill burstable bandwidth at the 95th or 98th percentile, cutting off the top 5% or 2% of peaks each month, so infrequent peaks are ignored and the customer is charged more fairly.
Monitoring data is often aggregated into a rate, average or percentile, and the 99th percentile response time over a small window, such as one minute, can give a very early signal of saturation.

notes: Statistics sections on the normal distribution, finance, medicine and the Excel and NumPy interpolation formulas were skipped; interviews need the idea and its use for latency and bandwidth.

title: Little's law

definition.text: Little's law states that the long-term average number of customers in a stable system equals the average arrival rate multiplied by the average time a customer spends in the system.

facts.text: The relationship is not influenced by the arrival process distribution, the service distribution or the service order; the only requirement is that the system be ergodic.
It applies to any system and to systems within systems: in a bank branch it holds for the customer line, for each teller and for the whole branch.
If the mean number in the system and the mean throughput are known, mean response time is their ratio: an average of ten jobs in the system at 50 per second gives 0.2 seconds.
A store with 10 arrivals per hour and an average stay of 0.5 hour holds 5 customers; at 20 arrivals per hour it must host 10 occupants or cut the stay to 0.25 hour.

A system is stable when arrivals match exits; if arrivals exceed exits the waiting grows without bound, and a system with limited space rejects the overflow, so its effective arrival rate is below the arrival rate.

Performance testers use it to check that results are not caused by bottlenecks in the test apparatus; on logged data its parameters must be estimated, since requests straddle the start and end of the interval.

notes: History of the proofs, the demography application and the distributional form were skipped.

title: Round-trip time

definition.text: Round-trip time is the time it takes to send a signal plus the time for its acknowledgement to come back, so it includes propagation on the path between the two endpoints.

facts.text: RTT is often measured with ping, though the payload and priority of ICMP messages may make ping time differ from the RTT other protocols experience; one-way end-to-end delay is often approximated as half the RTT.
RTT is twice the network latency plus a processing delay at the destination; network latency itself comprises processing delay in transmission, propagation time, transmission time and queueing time.

Propagation time depends on distance and transmission time is message size divided by bandwidth, so more bandwidth shrinks transmission time but not propagation, and the remaining delay is increasingly propagation.
Networks with both high bandwidth and high RTT hold large amounts of data in transit and need special protocol design, such as the TCP window scale option.

notes: TCP's smoothed RTT estimate and Jacobson/Karels, and Wi-Fi positioning, were left to mentions or skipped.
